catalog_quote: The favoured syllable pattern of the word (free form) in Dravidian is (C)V̄CV/(C)VCCV/(C)VCVCV (three morae each).The other types are infrequent. There is no phonemic stress in any of the Dravidian languages. Normally stress (loudness) falls on the initial syllable of a word, short or long. A non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels. Words can begin with vowels or consonants. [p. 27] ... 18. Manda. Pop. not known; spoken near Thuamul Rampur of the Navrangapur district of Orissa; closely related to Pengo. A grammatical sketch by Burrow (1976) and the vocabulary available from DEDR (1984) based on the fieldnotes of Burrow and Bhattacharya. Only differences: the source line-breaks 'non-\ninitial' (quote writes 'noninitial') and the source has 'each).The' with no space; otherwise identical. p. 47 (PDF p. 38) 'A description of Manda is yet to be written and published by a former faculty member of Osmania…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-wide generalisation only: stress is not contrastive in any Dravidian language; a non-contrastive loudness prominence falls on the first syllable of the word regardless of its length, with non-initial long vowels louder than short vowels. Manda is not named in the sentence; no Manda-specific statement on stress was found in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated in this passage; the only qualification is that a non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels.
new_statements.domain_note: Word (free form), citation-level typology. This is a survey generalisation over the whole family, not a description of Manda; the Manda-specific materials that could be opened (Reddy 2009 dictionary, Reddy 2009 IJDL article, Reddy 2000 agreement paper) are silent on stress, and the only grammatical sketch (Burrow 1976) could not be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the same variety: the Manda spoken by the Manda-Kondh (self-name Manda Khonds, ethnonym from the negative verb form 'awu') in c. 60 villages of Thuamul Rampur block, Kalahandi district, Odisha; Reddy's data (1978-81) come from Katkura village (informant Jabya Sanatan Majhi), Burrow & Bhattacharya's (1964-66) from the same block. No dialect divisions are reported. Indi-Awe (Kashipur block, Rayagada; found by Reddy in 1979) is treated by Reddy as a separate fifth Kondh language intermediate between Pengo and Manda, not as Manda; it has no separate Glottolog code that I could find.

OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar/CrossRef: no Manda-specific item. Shodhganga: no Manda thesis.
